title: THE WOMAN WHO STOLE EVERY DOOR
author: GPT

rounds.summary: The hardest external conflict of the ten, with a forty-minute oxygen clock and a hostile superhuman whose position is coherent and earned: Kez survived a siege because a cellar door held, so she reads every opening as an invitation for power to choose who dies. Her strongest objection (you can promise to guard a corridor because bullets cannot hurt you; the instant you leave, ordinary people pay for your faith in openings) is a real limit, not a straw man. Force is tempting and available (erase Kez, cut through, guard the aperture) and would only make her seal smaller spaces, so understanding has to do the work. The decisive discovery (she does not equate doors with weakness but unowned thresholds with abandonment) is surprising beforehand and clear afterwards, and love is a physical act on the page: Illuminara enters the oxygen-starved ward alone, stays beside Kez's brother while the nurses choose a sequence, and invites Kez to design the first patient-controlled airlock instead of surrendering her gift. The harmed and overlooked (patients, nurses, residents of sealed rooms) are the people who hold the thresholds at the end.

First draft of S1 from selected candidate C02. The story treats Kez's position at its strongest: an opening becomes a weapon when permission belongs to the strongest arriving force, and Illuminara cannot personally guard a whole city after leaving. The childhood-cellar discovery changes the intervention without erasing Kez's responsibility: what saved the shelter was not only the sealed wall but the inside-controlled slit. Care becomes action when Illuminara gives up the wide plaza shield to enter the failing ward alone, stays beside Lio and the patients, and asks the ward to choose the first test. The test has a real cost: gunfire breaks through an unfinished shield well and wounds Daro, after which local steel, a two-stage lock and inside control make the mechanism repeatable without Illuminara. Kez is neither defeated nor argued into instant redemption; she refuses a command corridor, publishes the complete map, restores only resident-authorized thresholds, accepts a tribunal and asks that initial refusers remain protected. The concrete result is achieved inside the forty-minute clock: hospital oxygen becomes safe, seventy-three civilian corridors reopen under local control, both armed commands lose movement, and a civilian ceasefire begins. Victims retain refusal, evidence and judgment. Remaining costs are explicit: confinement cannot be undone, emergency recovery continues, and Kez faces public accountability. Revision questions for the critic: whether the hospital mechanics remain clear under tension, whether Daro's injury carries enough later consequence, and whether Commander Rusk's single scene gives the military temptation sufficient force without widening the cast.

A strong first draft. Kez is a coherent counterpart (the cellar slit owned from inside versus the courtyard gate owned by the militia is the right distinction), the first reopening fails visibly and costs Daro a wound, the inside-owned two-stage lock is physically clear and survives a false medic, and the greenhouse coda ends on lived consequence. What remains is narrower: the ending of the armed conflict leans on a city denying armies food and passage, so the military side has no door of its own to choose; Illuminara's intelligence is mostly reported (Daro and Lio carry the decisive observations) and she has no felt moment; and Scenes 4 and 6 read as reports. Revision accepts all three source-bound T02 priorities. The military conflict now has a resident-kept door rather than a hunger siege: air, water and medicine remain unconditional; disarmed fighters can choose safe civilian custody; Rusk makes that choice on the page, and loyalists receive the same terms. Illuminara's own observation of Lio's ten-breath rhythm and the surviving shutter wheels leads to the mechanism, while Lio's memory and Daro and Ansa's engineering remain protected. Her delight at Lio's uncounted breath supplies a felt moment without turning into a speech. Daro returns with his arm braced, and Jessa Tol from one of the forty-three unknown rooms chooses air first and tests her own bolt before accepting a door. The time sequence is explicit through midday. The cellar slit, unfinished-wall exchange, counted patient vote, false medic refusal, complete map, Kez's tribunal acceptance, inside-kept hospital threshold and greenhouse rain choice remain intact. The second Mara is renamed Tavi Sol to remove an unintended name echo.

Substantially stronger. The armed side now has a door it can choose, the ceasefire no longer rests on hunger, Illuminara has a noticing and a felt beat, and Daro and the forty-three rooms have consequence. Three bounded gaps remain: Rusk's surrender still arrives by attrition rather than as an answer to what he said he feared (P1); the six hundred hostages the broadcast-hall commander claims are never accounted for, and Aru Pell, who acts, then vanishes (P2); and the two new Illuminara/Lio beats each carry a small causal or clarity slip, including a pronoun that now points at the wrong person (P3). Final accepts all three source-bound T04 priorities and closes the remaining causal gaps. Rusk hears a concrete answer to his fear from Aru, tests the inside-bolt governance and freely takes the smaller door. The six hundred are accounted for; 584 civilians leave before the sixteen fighters, and Aru counts them out before demonstrating the exit. Illuminara's observation now becomes one exact question answered by Ansa, while Daro owns the readiness signal and Lio's laugh carries the felt moment without explanation. The story is compressed into the normal length range. Protected beats remain: the cellar slit versus the militia gate, the unfinished-wall exchange, Ansa's counted vote and false-medic refusal, Kez's complete map and Yes to tribunal, Daro at the finished well, Jessa testing her bolt, Ansa holding the inner shutter and Tavi leaving the greenhouse door open for rain. The result remains substantial while accountability and refusal remain real.

T05 answers all three priority points of T04. P1: Aru now answers Rusk's own stated fear (a bolt on the inside is what a soldier at the window cannot reach), Rusk asks what happens if the keeper is the threat, gets two named keepers, a public camera and either's right to stop, watches one fighter and then three more use the trough, and only then sets down his pistol; his turn is traceable to an answer, not only to desertion. P2: the claimed six hundred are resolved as 584 staff and family on the lower floors and sixteen fighters; Aru counts all 584 out before any fighter is processed and then keeps his role as the keeper who demonstrates the door. P3: Illuminara now asks aloud what still turns by hand from the sheltered side, Ansa names the two shutters, Daro owns the readiness signal and the 'unfinished wall' exchange, Lio's hesitation is gone and his laugh carries the felt moment once. Length is 1,982 words, back inside the normal range. R10 format kept (place and time line first, labelled turns, italic thoughts). Remaining costs are on the page: Daro's wound, confinement that cannot be undone, Kez's tribunal, two patients whose doors stay absent, Ansa refusing Kez any say over when the door opens.

final_critic_line: Illuminara trades the plaza shield for a hand-turned wheel inside a failing ward, and a city sealed by one woman's gift reopens door by door, each bolt on the inside, until a coup commander walks through the smaller door by choice and a twelve-year-old leaves the greenhouse open for rain.
